slides.title: Electricity: Magnetic and Heating Effects
slides.subtitle: At the science fair, an iron nail wrapped in wire lifts paper clips like a magnet — yet there's no magnet anywhere, only a closed circuit. How?
points: Without a lamp, is there another way to tell that current is flowing in a circuit?
Is it possible to make temporary magnets? How can these be made?
We make heat by burning fuel — but how is heat generated inside electrical appliances?
How do we know if a cell or battery is dead, and can all of them be recharged?

slides.title: Does an electric current have a magnetic effect?
slides.intro: Sumana's lifting-electromagnet model had no magnet, only a circuit. To explain it, we start with a compass and a single live wire.

slides.title: A compass beneath a live wire
slides.purpose: We want to find out whether a current-carrying wire can affect a **magnetic compass** — a hidden way to detect current even without a lamp.
steps: Build — fix two nails on cardboard and stretch a wire between them, just above the surface
Wire up — connect the wire to a cell through a homemade switch
Place — set a magnetic compass right beneath the wire
Switch — flick ON then OFF a few times, watching the needle each time
slides.observe: Switch **ON** and the needle **deflects** from its rest direction; switch **OFF** and it swings back. The current is doing something to the compass — even though the wire is not a magnet.

slides.title: A current makes a magnetic field
slides.body: A compass needle is a tiny magnet, so its deflection means the wire has a **magnetic effect**. When electric current flows through a conductor it produces a **magnetic field** around it — the **magnetic effect of electric current**. The region where this effect can be felt is the **magnetic field**, and it disappears the instant the current stops.

slides.translation: Demonstrating to his class in Denmark, Ørsted noticed that whenever a circuit was closed or opened, a nearby compass needle deflected. He investigated until he was certain a current produces a magnetic field, then published — the first proof that electricity and magnetism are linked.

slides.title: Electromagnets
slides.intro: The magnetic effect powers electric bells, motors, fans, and loudspeakers. But it also answers Sumana's puzzle — so what happens when we wind that wire into a coil around an iron nail?

slides.title: A nail that grabs paper clips
slides.purpose: We test whether a coil of current-carrying wire can turn an ordinary iron nail into a **temporary magnet**.
steps: Wind — wrap about 50 cm of insulated wire tightly around an iron nail as a coil
Connect — join the wire ends to a cell for just a few seconds, or the cell weakens
Lift — bring the nail to some iron paper clips
Cut off — disconnect the wire and watch the clips
slides.observe: While current flows, the clips **cling** to the nail; the moment you disconnect, they **fall off**. The nail is a magnet only as long as the current flows.

slides.title: Build a coil and test its core
slides.purpose: We investigate the effect carefully: does a bare coil deflect a compass, and what does adding an **iron core** change?
steps: Coil — wind about 50 turns of insulated wire on a paper cylinder
Watch — place compasses at both ends, connect the cell, look for deflection
Disconnect — check that the needles return to rest
Add a core — slide an iron nail into the cylinder and repeat, then offer it some clips
slides.observe: The bare coil already deflects the needles. With an **iron nail** inside, the deflection is **much greater** and the nail now grabs clips too. Stop the current and the coil loses its magnetism.

slides.title: This is an electromagnet
slides.body: A **current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet** is called an **electromagnet**. Inserting an **iron core** makes it far stronger, which is why most practical electromagnets are built around iron. Unlike a permanent magnet, it is magnetic **only while current flows** — a magnet you can switch on and off.

slides.title: Does it have two poles?
slides.purpose: A bar magnet has a North and a South pole. We check whether our electromagnet does too — and how to name them.
steps: Label — mark the two ends of the coil A and B
Probe A — bring a compass to end A, connect the cell, note which pole is attracted
Reason — unlike poles attract, so if the compass's North is pulled to A, then A is South
Probe B — repeat at end B and compare
slides.observe: End A attracts one pole, end B the **opposite** pole. Just like a bar magnet, an electromagnet has **two poles — North and South**.

slides.title: What makes it stronger?
slides.body: Repeating the activity with changes shows what controls an electromagnet's strength. A single cell gives a **weak** field, so little deflection and few clips. **More cells** mean more current and a stronger magnet; **more turns** in the coil also strengthen it. And reversing the current's direction **swaps the poles**.

slides.title: Three dials you can turn
rows: Stronger field, more deflection, more clips

slides.title: Earth is a giant electromagnet
slides.body: A freely hung magnet settles **north–south** because Earth itself acts like a magnet. Deep in the core, the **movement of liquid iron** sets up electric currents that generate Earth's magnetic field. Migratory birds, fish, and animals navigate by it, and it **shields** life from harmful particles arriving from space.

slides.title: Lifting electromagnets
slides.intro: From a fairground model to the factory floor — the same on/off magnet that grabbed paper clips can move tonnes of steel.

slides.title: Switch it on to grab, off to drop
slides.body: Strong electromagnets hung from cranes are **lifting electromagnets**. Switch the current **ON** and the magnet seizes iron and steel; switch it **OFF** and the field vanishes, releasing the load — widely used in **factories and scrap yards** to move and sort heavy metal. And the link runs both ways: just as a current makes a field, a **moving magnet can produce a current**, the basis of motors and power generators you'll meet in higher grades.

slides.title: Does a current-carrying wire get hot?
slides.intro: While making the electromagnet, the wire ends grew warm. That warmth is a second effect of current — and the principle behind every heating appliance.

slides.title: Warming a nichrome wire
slides.purpose: We test directly whether passing current through a wire **heats** it, using a special high-resistance wire called **nichrome**.
steps: Mount — fix two nails about 5 cm apart on cardboard and tie a 10 cm, 0.3 mm nichrome wire between them
Feel first — with the switch OFF, touch the wire
Switch on — flow current for about 30 s, then switch OFF
Feel again — touch the wire only momentarily (never hold it)
slides.observe: After the current, the wire feels **warm**. Pushing current through a conductor produces heat — the **heating effect of electric current**. (Safety first: never touch the wire for long.)

slides.title: Resistance turns current into heat
slides.body: Every conductor offers some **resistance** to current, and different materials resist differently. **Nichrome** resists far more than copper of the same size and length. That resistance converts some of the **electrical energy into heat energy**, so the wire warms up. The more it resists, the more it heats.

slides.title: How much heat? It depends
slides.body: Repeating the activity with a **2-cell battery** produces noticeably more heat than one cell. The heat generated depends on the **magnitude of the current**, and also on the wire's **material**, its **thickness** and **length**, and the **duration** for which current flows. (Always do this under a teacher's supervision.)

slides.title: Where the heating effect works for us
slides.body: Each device hides a **heating element** — a rod or coil of wire that heats up, sometimes glowing red hot. It's the same principle that makes an incandescent lamp's filament glow:

slides.title: When heat helps and when it harms
slides.leftBody: In steel industries a high-temperature **furnace** uses current's heat to melt and recycle scrap steel into usable steel — a major industrial use of the heating effect.
slides.rightBody: Overheating wastes energy in transmission and can melt plugs and sockets or even start fires. Use wires, plugs, and sockets **rated** for the current, plus safety devices in the circuit.

slides.title: How does a battery generate electricity?
slides.intro: Cells and batteries lit our lamp, made our magnet, and heated our wire. So what is inside them that produces electricity? We start with the earliest cell ever made.

slides.title: Voltaic cell
slides.intro: The first true electric cell — two different metals and a liquid, quietly turning chemistry into current.

slides.title: Two metals and an electrolyte
slides.body: A **Voltaic cell** (also called a Galvanic cell) holds two rods of **different metals**, the **electrodes**, dipped in a liquid **electrolyte** — usually a weak acid or salt solution. A **chemical reaction** between rods and electrolyte produces electricity, driving current from the positive to the negative terminal. When the chemicals are used up, the cell goes **'dead'**.

slides.transliteration: A frog's leg and the first battery
slides.translation: Galvani saw a dead frog's leg kick when touched with copper and iron, and thought the electricity came from the frog. Volta disagreed — he replaced the leg with saltwater-soaked paper and still got a current, proving it was the metals and liquid that made electricity. The result: the first battery.

slides.title: A battery made of lemons
slides.purpose: We build our own Voltaic cell from kitchen materials, proving that **different metals in a juicy electrolyte** really can generate current.
steps: Insert — push a copper wire and an iron nail into each of five or six lemons, kept apart
Chain — join the copper of one lemon to the nail of the next, all in a row
Connect — wire an LED between the first copper and the last nail
Fix polarity — if the LED stays dark, reverse its connections
slides.observe: The **LED glows**, proving the cell works. The **copper and iron are the electrodes**, and the **lemon juice is the electrolyte** that conducts. A salt solution would work just as well.

slides.title: Why some metals go positive
slides.body: Many metal pairs make Voltaic cells — **zinc/copper, aluminium/copper, magnesium/copper, lead/copper**, and more. Some metals, like **copper**, tend to act as the **positive** electrode; others, like **zinc**, as the **negative**. This comes down to their chemical properties, which you'll study further in higher grades.

slides.title: Dry cells
slides.intro: Voltaic cells were a breakthrough, but sloshing liquid isn't handy for a torch. The fix: replace the liquid with a paste.

slides.title: Liquid swapped for a paste
slides.body: A **dry cell** is 'dry' because its electrolyte is a thick **moist paste**, not a liquid. A **zinc container** forms the negative terminal, and a central **carbon rod** capped with metal is the positive terminal, surrounded by the paste. It is **single-use** — once spent, it must be disposed of, which is why rechargeable batteries are taking over.

slides.title: Rechargeable batteries
slides.intro: What if a spent battery didn't have to be thrown away — but simply refilled with energy and used again?

slides.title: Batteries you can charge again
slides.body: **Rechargeable batteries** can be recharged and reused many times, cutting waste and saving money. They range from tiny cells in **watches and phones** to large ones in **laptops, inverters, and electric vehicles**. They don't last forever, though — after many charge cycles they slowly **wear out**, which is why an old phone needs charging more often.

slides.title: Lithium-ion, and what comes next
slides.body: Today's most common rechargeable is the **lithium-ion** battery, found in almost every battery device. It relies on scarce metals like **lithium and cobalt**, so nations race to secure, recycle, and replace them. Even a 'dead' battery still holds valuable acids and metals — so it belongs in an **e-waste** facility, not the bin. Scientists are now developing **solid-state** batteries — safer, faster-charging, longer-lasting — for a cleaner energy future.

slides.title: Words from this chapter
slides.body: The vocabulary of magnetic and heating effects:

slides.title: One circuit, three powers
slides.subtitle: Current makes magnetism, current makes heat, and chemistry makes current — from Ørsted's twitching compass to a crane's lifting magnet, a glowing kettle coil, and a lemon that lights an LED.
